analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for workers to unionize and raises penalties on employers who violate labor law.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 224-194 in February 2020, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the nation's main labor law to make union organizing easier and employer violations costlier. It would prevent employers from classifying workers as independent contractors or supervisors to keep them outside labor-law protections, ban permanently replacing strikers, and make it an unfair labor practice to force employees to attend meetings aimed at discouraging union membership. It would also raise fines for violations to as much as $50,000 each ($100,000 for repeat offenders), let workers sue and collect double damages, override state "right-to-work" laws so union contracts can require fees from all covered workers, and send stalled first contracts to binding arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to join or form a union gain stronger legal protection and real penalties for employers who fire or retaliate against them. Gig and contract workers classified as independent contractors would gain collective-bargaining rights. Existing union members gain from overrides of state right-to-work laws and from stronger remedies when employers violate the law.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers seeking to organize and union members

how_it_helps.text: Redefines who counts as an employee, supervisor, and joint employer so employers cannot classify workers out of labor-law protections, including gig workers treated as independent contractors.
Makes it an unfair labor practice to permanently replace or discriminate against workers who strike, and to require employees to attend employer meetings designed to discourage union membership.

Raises the stakes for violations: civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation (doubled to $100,000 for repeat discharge violations), back pay with no reductions, liquidated damages of two times actual damages, punitive damages, and a private right of action letting workers sue in court.
Prohibits employers from requiring workers to sign agreements waiving their right to join class or collective lawsuits over workplace disputes, voiding such mandatory-arbitration clauses.

Allows collective-bargaining agreements to require all covered employees to pay fees for representation notwithstanding contrary state right-to-work laws, and permits secondary strikes by workers at other companies.
Speeds up union elections and, if a first contract stalls, requires mediation and then binding arbitration, with the arbitrator's decision binding for two years.

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the cost: higher fines and damages for violations, loss of mandatory-arbitration clauses, joint liability under franchising and contracting arrangements, possible reclassification of contractor workforces (a particular concern for gig platforms), and compelled fee arrangements in right-to-work states. Unions would gain fee revenue in right-to-work states; some workers who prefer not to pay fees or who value independent-contractor flexibility would lose options. The public pays indirectly through higher prices where labor costs rise, and modestly through NLRB enforcement.

drawbacks.text: The fair-share provision would override right-to-work laws in more than half the states, requiring employees in covered bargaining units to pay union fees as a condition of employment even if they decline to join.

Binding arbitration of first contracts takes bargaining out of the parties' hands: if mediation fails after 90 days plus a 30-day mediation window, a three-member panel sets wages and terms binding for two years, based partly on employees' cost of living and comparable employers' pay.

Employers would have no standing to participate in union representation proceedings before the NLRB, and if an employer interferes with an election the Board could certify the union and order bargaining without a new vote.

The narrow independent-contractor test would reclassify many gig and freelance workers as employees, which critics argue would cost some of them flexibility and work opportunities; the joint-employer definition would also expose franchisors and lead firms to liability for workers they do not directly employ.

Penalties of up to $50,000 per violation ($100,000 for repeat offenders) and personal liability for directors and officers would significantly raise legal exposure, falling hardest on smaller employers with less capacity to absorb disputes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the bill addresses a real and well-documented problem: labor-law penalties have been too small to deter employers from firing union supporters, and elections can drag out while employers campaign against the union. The organizing, anti-striker-replacement, penalty, and mandatory-arbitration provisions are substantial gains for employees. The costs are real too: overriding state right-to-work laws is a significant national policy choice that compels fees from objecting workers, binding arbitration substitutes a panel's decision for negotiation, and reclassification under the contractor test would change how millions of gig and freelance workers engage with work. Whether the trade is worth it depends on how much weight one puts on collective bargaining rights versus individual contracting choice; the bill comes down clearly on the side of the former.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in February 2020 on a mostly party-line vote, but the Senate sent it to its labor committee and never voted on it before that Congress ended, killing the bill.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 2, 2019 and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor, chaired by the bill's sponsor.
The committee approved an amended version on a 26-21 vote and reported it on December 16, 2019.
On final passage, the House approved the bill 224-194, with 219 of 226 voting Democrats in favor and only 5 of 191 voting Republicans; an effort to recommit the bill with instructions failed 195-223.

The Senate received the bill on February 10, 2020 and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where no further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill had 218 cosponsors at introduction-stage support (216 Democrats, 2 Republicans), giving it a House majority before it was reported.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and business groups that opposed the bill are better off: because the Senate never voted, labor-law penalties remain low, right-to-work laws stand unchallenged, and employers keep mandatory-arbitration clauses and the current election process. Union-avoidance strategies that depend on those rules stay intact.

for.name: Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott
for.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, guided it through his committee (reported amended 26-21), and managed it to House passage.

for.name: House Democratic caucus
for.what_they_did: Voted nearly unanimously for final passage (219-7), supplying almost all of the 224 yes votes.

for.name: 218 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors before the bill reached the floor, giving it a House majority on paper.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote after the House passed it; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republican bloc
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill and supported leaving it in committee rather than bringing it to a vote.

against.name: 190 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against final passage 186-5, and 192 Republicans backed the motion to recommit with instructions.

against.name: Business and employer groups
against.role: Opposing coalition (e.g., the U.S. Chamber of Commerce)
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the bill as a top legislative priority, arguing it would raise costs, override right-to-work laws, and upend the gig economy.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split almost entirely by party: 219 Democrats voted yes and 7 no, while 5 Republicans voted yes and 186 no; the motion to recommit was 192 Republicans and 3 Democrats for, all other Democrats against.
